Yes, the story (which is the famous opening of Franz Kafka's *The Metamorphosis*) has an appropriate and masterful balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative seamlessly weaves real-time dramatization (scene) with background information (exposition). The "scene" elements ground the reader in the bizarre present moment: Gregor waking up, examining his new insect body, struggling to roll onto his right side, itching his stomach, and panicking as he looks at the ticking alarm clock. Interspersed within these real-time actions are "exposition" elements delivered through Gregor's internal monologue and observations of his room. Through this exposition, the reader learns crucial background details—that he is an exhausted traveling fabric salesman, that he hates his boss, and that he is only working this job to pay off his parents' debt. 

This balance is particularly effective because the mundane exposition about his job contrasts sharply with the surreal scene of his physical transformation, heightening the tension and absurdity of the story while keeping the reader fully engaged. Note: While the question contains two parts, "Yes" here confirms the first proposition—that the story achieves an appropriate balance rather than relying too heavily on one element.
